red_flags.text: A coronary stent placed recently, or an acute coronary syndrome within the past year: stopping antiplatelet therapy risks stent thrombosis, which is frequently fatal.
Mechanical heart valve, especially mitral, or a venous thromboembolism within the last three months: high thrombotic risk.
Planned neuraxial or deep regional block: the interruption intervals are longer than for surgery alone.
Impaired renal function with dabigatran, which prolongs its effect substantially.
An emergency operation on a patient who took an anticoagulant today: this is a reversal decision, not an interruption plan.

do_now.text: Record every antithrombotic, its indication, the dose, the time of the last dose, and the stent type and date, at pre-assessment, not on the morning of surgery.
Classify the procedure's bleeding risk (minimal, low to moderate, or high) and the patient's thrombotic risk before deciding anything.
Do not stop antiplatelet therapy in a patient with a recent coronary stent without discussion with the cardiologist; defer elective surgery instead where possible.
Emergency surgery on an anticoagulant: reverse according to the agent and the local protocol, and involve haematology.

assess.text: Thrombotic risk: indication for anticoagulation, stroke risk in atrial fibrillation, valve type and position, and timing of any venous thromboembolism.
Bleeding risk of the patient and the procedure. Minimal-risk procedures, such as many dental, skin and cataract procedures, can often proceed without interruption.
Renal function by Cockcroft-Gault creatinine clearance, which determines DOAC interruption intervals, particularly for dabigatran.
Cardiac risk of the surgery itself.

investigate.text: Routine pre-operative coagulation testing is not needed after a standardised DOAC interruption; in PAUSE most patients had minimal residual levels.
INR the day before surgery for patients stopping warfarin; a low dose of vitamin K may be given if it remains raised.
Renal function and full blood count at pre-assessment.

resuscitate.text: Apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban: omit for 1 day before a low to moderate bleeding-risk procedure and 2 days before a high bleeding-risk procedure, with no bridging.

Dabigatran with creatinine clearance 50 mL/min or more: omit for 1 day before low to moderate and 2 days before high bleeding-risk procedures. With clearance below 50 mL/min: omit for 2 days and 4 days respectively.
Warfarin: stop 5 days before surgery. Heparin bridging is not recommended for most patients with atrial fibrillation, because it increased bleeding without reducing thromboembolism.
Consider bridging only for high thrombotic risk on warfarin, such as a mechanical mitral valve, decided with the specialist responsible.
Neuraxial anaesthesia: follow ASRA intervals, which for apixaban, rivaroxaban and edoxaban are generally 72 hours, longer than the surgical interruption.

definitive.text: Aspirin: continue in most patients having non-cardiac surgery, particularly for secondary prevention; stop it only for procedures where even minor bleeding is catastrophic, such as some intracranial, spinal or posterior eye surgery.
P2Y12 inhibitors when interruption is agreed: clopidogrel 5 days, ticagrelor 3 to 5 days, prasugrel 7 days before surgery.
Restart DOACs 1 day after a low to moderate bleeding-risk procedure and 2 to 3 days after a high bleeding-risk procedure, once haemostasis is secure.
Restart warfarin within about 24 hours after surgery when haemostasis allows; resume P2Y12 inhibitors within about 24 hours when haemostasis allows, per the cardiology plan.
Give pharmacological VTE prophylaxis between surgery and full-dose resumption when there is a gap, per local protocol.

escalate.text: Cardiology for any patient with a coronary stent or recent acute coronary syndrome, before the date of surgery is fixed.
Haematology for mechanical valves, recent venous thromboembolism, thrombophilia, or reversal in emergencies.
Anaesthesia early when regional or neuraxial anaesthesia is planned.
Write the plan with dates in the notes and give it to the patient in writing. Most errors are of execution, not of decision.

notes: Bridging feels safe and is not. In atrial fibrillation it more than doubled major bleeding without reducing arterial thromboembolism.
DOAC interruption is a matter of days and depends on bleeding risk and, for dabigatran, renal function. A standard schedule makes routine coagulation tests unnecessary.
The patient on a recent coronary stent is the one in whom a well-meaning surgical team can cause a death by stopping a tablet. Ask the stent date every time.
